en: Abhidhānottara 12 = palm-leaf manuscript = Raghu Vīra’s manuscript reproduction by Lokesh Chandra
Now I shall explain the Yoga that accomplishes all desires and purposes, which is higher than even the highest,
the sovereignty of Vārāhī, which swiftly bestows accomplishment upon the Yoginīs.
This is the compendium of the essential yoga of all yogas.

One should draw an eight-petalled lotus of the most excellent and various colors, filled with a pericarp and filaments; this is the practice performed with total purity. In its center is the digit-moon, transparent and naturally stainless.
Above that, one should visualize the vowels and consonants (ālikāli), adorned in the center with the syllable *vaṃ*.
From the midst of that, the goddess Vārāhī-Vajrayoginī arises—
four-faced, twelve-armed, three-eyed, and intensely passionate.
Seated in the half-lotus posture, she was dancing, exceedingly beautiful.
Naked, with disheveled hair, her face that of Ardhanārīśvara,
bearing a form of blue and red colors, fierce with a crown of skulls,
her hands busily holding a vajra and a bell, she abides in the turning of the lotus.
On her forehead is the flame-gesture (jvālāmudrā), and she has a human skin as an upper garment;

she holds a skull-cup and a khaṭvāṅga staff, while her other hands hold a noose and a goad; she also carries a hand-drum, a curved knife, and a severed head, and possesses four faces, the first of which is that of Brahmā.
Adorned with divine faces of blue, yellow, green, and other colors;
her face made terrifying by protruding fangs and graced by a crescent moon;
bearing upon her head a crown marked with a double vajra; the bestower of all spiritual accomplishments.
The goddess is sealed with the six mudrās, her girdle adorned with jeweled pendants;
she is beautified by the tinkling sound of her girdle and the jingling of her anklets,
and she shines with armlets and a garland of diamonds upon her forehead.
On the eastern petal is the Ḍākinī, marked with a vajra, beautiful in form and enchanting;
on the left is the goddess Lāmā, with a boar’s face, terrifying and formidable.
In the west is the elephant-faced goddess Khaṇḍarohā, who is Raudriṇī;
in the south is the goddess Rūpiṇī, whose fierce form has the face of a horse;
she is three-eyed and possesses a universal form.
She holds a skull-cup and a khaṭvāṅga staff; another holds a severed head. She should be naked with disheveled hair, dancing and exquisitely beautiful.
Seated upon the back of a corpse in the half-lotus posture, she is formidable, fierce, and terrifying.
Bhairava and Kālarātrī were placed at the soles of the Goddess's feet.
In the four corners, beginning with the southeast, vessels containing the *bodhicitta* and other substances—
resembling conchs, jasmine flowers, and the moon— were arranged upon the ritual jars.
In the eastern, northern, and other directions, one should draw a six-cornered wheel (*ṣaṭkoṇa-cakra*).
In the center of the wheel, the wise one should write the four families of the foremost [deities]:
Māmakī, Locanā, Tārā, and Pāṇḍaravāsinī.
The goddess who is the mistress of the Vajra family is blue, white, and red;
the goddess who delights the Śāśvata family is white, blue, and reddish-brown;
and the goddess born of the Karma family is green, white, and red.
The goddess born from the Lotus family is red, yellow, and green;
she has three eyes, loose hair, and wears no clothes. She is complete with all ornaments and adorned with the six mudrās.
Holding skull-bowls and khaṭvāṅgas as their emblems, they are of four kinds;
they hold respectively the vajra, the wheel, the viśvavajra, and the supreme red lotus.
Likewise, all of them hold bells and abide within the whorl of a lotus.
Trampled by the feet of the four Mothers, her face dancing and laughing,
she stands in the center of a universal lotus and moon; she bestows the accomplishments of the Kula,
holding a severed head and a *ḍamaru* drum in her hands, and is beautifully adorned with a vajra and a flaying knife.
[One should visualize her] wearing a crown of a garland of skulls and adorned with a wreath of severed heads;
one should arrange the sequence of seats and so forth in all the corner sections. In the eastern [section], one should place the divine [deities] according to their order upon the six-cornered wheel.
In the first corner, at Pullīramalaya, is Pracaṇḍā; in the second, at Jālandhara, is Caṇḍākṣī;
and in the third, at Oḍiyāna, is Prabhāvatī.
In the fourth, Arbuda, is Mahānāsā; in the fifth, Godāvarī, is Vīramatī;
in the sixth, Rāmeśvara, is Kharvarī.
In the second northern wheel, which has six spokes: in the first spoke, at Devikoṭa, is Laṅkeśvarī;
in the second, at Mālava, is Drumacchāyā;
in the third, at Kāmarūpa, is Airāvatī.
In the fourth, Oḍra, is Mahābhairavā;
in the fifth, Triśakuni, is Vāyuvegā;
and in the sixth, Kosala, is Surābhakṣī.
In the western six-spoked [wheel], the third circle: in the east, Kaliṅga, is Śyāmādevī;
in the second, Lampāka, is Subhadrā;
in the third, Kāñcika, is Hayakarṇā.
In the fourth [region], on the Himalaya, is Khagānanā;
in the fifth, in Pretapurī, is Cakravegā;
in the sixth, at Gṛhadevatā, is Khaṇḍarohā.
In the six-spoked wheel on the right: in the east is Śauṇḍinī;
in the second, Suvarṇadvīpa, is Cakravarmiṇī;
in the third, Nagara, is Suvīrā.
In the fourth [region], Sindhu, she is Mahābalā;
in the fifth, Maru, she is Cakravartinī;
in the sixth, Kulatā, she is Mahāvīryā.

In the first [direction], white and green; [they hold] a skull-cup, a khaṭvāṅga, a wheel, a ḍamaru, and a flaying-knife. In the second, the north, blue and yellow; [they hold] a vajra, a skull-cup, a khaṭvāṅga, a ḍamaru, and a flaying-knife.
In the third, the west, red and yellow; [they hold] a skull-cup, a khaṭvāṅga, a lotus, a ḍamaru, and a flaying-knife.
In the fourth [position] to the right of the Goddess is Pītaraktā, who holds a double-vajra, a *ḍamaru* drum, a flaying knife, a skull-cup, and a *khaṭvāṅga*.

All the goddesses are half-female Śiva (Ardhanārīśvara), three-eyed, four-armed, naked, with disheveled hair, standing in the dancing posture (*ardhaparyaṅka*) upon a corpse seat (*pretapṛṣṭhāsana*). They wear crowns of skull garlands and are adorned with the five mudrās. They are further adorned with anklets, girdles, and armlets marked with vajras.
Then, having surrounded the exterior, there is a wheel (*cakra*) and a vajra-garland to the east;
to the north and west of the wheel-garland, there is a double-vajra (*viśvavajra*) garland.
To the south [of the central deity] is a row of lotuses; in the center, it is beautifully adorned with a row of vajras.
In all the corner sections, one should draw the nature of the double-vajra (viśvavajra).
Outside of that, the wise one should encircle it with a row of corpses ending in double-vajras.
On the outside, at the gates of the mandala and in the four corner regions,
one who is composed should place the Ḍākinīs of fierce form;
Kākāsyā, blue and red and captivating, is placed in the east.
At the northern gate is Ulūkāsyā, beautiful with green and red;
at the western gate is Śvānāsyā, fierce with yellow and smoke-colored extremities;
and at the southern [gate] is Sūkarāsyā, having a green and blue form.
She has three eyes, a distorted appearance, and is fierce; another [form] is naked and wears no clothing.
She is squinting, short in stature, and stands in the *mālinī* posture upon the center of a universal lotus and sun disk, adorned with the five mudrās.
Vibhramā, wearing a crown of skulls and with disheveled hair,
has the face of a buffalo and is stationed in the southeastern direction;
Yamadūtī, with the face of a donkey, is stationed in the southwestern direction.
Yamadaṃṣṭrī, born of Rudra, with the face of a camel, is situated in the northwestern direction;
Yamamathanī, with the face of a horse, is distressed and stationed in the northeastern direction;
she wears a crown of garlands of skulls, possesses universal forms, and is captivating to the mind.
Naked, with disheveled hair, dancing in the half-lotus posture,
her face terrifying with fangs, three-eyed, and with a flickering countenance;
she stands in the center of a sun disc upon a universal lotus, overwhelmed by the intensity of passion.
All the retinues and maṇḍala-deities are situated above the hungry ghosts.
She holds a skull-cup and a khaṭvāṅga staff, and carries a flaying knife and a severed head;
she is most terrifying, playing a hand-drum with her right hand.
Outside, there is a rampart of skulls, and it exists in many other ways as well.
With offerings of song and dance, with various supreme commitments, with flowers, incense, lamps, and so forth, with perfumes, garlands,
and ointments, with celestial garments and palaces, and with the most excellent of divine musical instruments.
One should worship [the goddesses] surrounded on all sides by the outer yoginīs;
these and others, infinite in number, fill the entire expanse of space (*khadhātu*). One should thus worship the yoga of the yoginīs, the supreme *Vārāhyabhyudaya*.
One should not reveal this supreme secret to just anyone.
On the outside, one should visualize the garland of pretas within the most excellent maṇḍala;
in this manner, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa), placing it according to the proper sequence.
Pracaṇḍā resides in the nails and teeth; Caṇḍākṣī in the hair of the head and body;
and Prabhāvatī in the skin and impurities.
Māṃsā is Mahānāsā; Snāyū is Vīramatī; Asthi is Kharvarī.
Bukke is Laṅkeśvarī;
Drumacchāyā is in the heart;
Airāvatī is in the eyes.
In the bile is Mahābhairavā; Phupphusa is Vāyuvegā;
in the intestines is Surābhakṣī.
Śyāmādevī [is the womb] of the two virtuous ones; Subhadrā is the belly;
Hayakarṇā is the excrement.
Sīmāntā is Khagānanā; Śleṣmā is Cakravegā;
Pūṣan is Khaṇḍarohā.
Śauṇḍinī [offered] blood;
Cakravarmiṇī, sweat;
Suvīrā, fat.
Tears are Mahābalā; phlegm is Cakravartinī;
snot is Mahāvīryā.
Pracaṇḍā is at the summit of Pullīramalaya; Caṇḍākṣī is at Jālandhara on the crest-lock;
Prabhāvatī is at Oḍiyāna on the right ear.
Arbudi is on the back; Mahānāsā is at the base of the spine; Godāvarī is in the left ear; Vīramatī is between the eyebrows at Rāmeśvara; and Kharvarī is [in the right ear].
Lankeśvarī is at Devikoṭa-cakṣus;
Drumacchāyā is on the two shoulders of Mālava; Airāvatī is at the two armpits of Kāmarūpa.
Mahābhairavā is at Oḍra, on the pair of breasts;
Vāyuvegā is at Triśakuni, at the navel; Surābhakṣī is at Kosala, at the tip of the nose.
Śyāmādevī is at the mouth of Kaliṅga;
Subhadrā is at the throat of Lampāka;
Hayakarṇā is at the heart of Kāñcī.
Khagānanā is at the penis of the Himālaya; Cakravegā is at the secret organ of Pretapurī;
Khaṇḍarohā is at the anus of Gṛhadevatā.
Saurāṣṭrā is on the two thighs;
Śauṇḍinī is on the two shanks born of Suvarṇadvīpa; Cakravarmiṇī is on the feet; and Suvīrā is on the fingers of the hands.
Mahābalā is on the back of the Sindhu tree;
Cakravartinī is at Maruaṅguya;
Suvīrā is at the two knees of Kulatā.
The earth element is the caster down; the water element is the slayer;
fire is the attractor.
The wind element is Narteśvarī;
the space element is Padmajālinī;
and in the aggregate of form is Vairocana.
In the aggregate of feeling is Vajrasūrya; in the aggregate of perception is Padmanarteśvara;
in the aggregate of mental formations is Vajrarāja.
In the aggregate of consciousness is Vajrasattva;
in the state of all Tathāgatas is Śrī Herukavajra;
in the eye is Mohavajra.
In the two ears is Dveṣavajra;
in the nose, Īrṣyāvajra; and in the mouth, Rāgavajra.
In touch, Mātsaryavajra;
in all sense bases, Aiśvaryavajra; in the mind, Akṣobhyavajra.
Speech is Amitavajra;
in the body is Vairocanavajra.
One should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) in this manner; he beholds the wheel of gnosis (*jñānacakra*).
He undertakes yoga, and his entire being becomes that [wheel].
One should meditate upon the occasion of consecration and worship as having been made of one flavor (*samarasīkṛta*).

In his heart, with the essences of the offerings and the nectar of gnosis, he should recite the mantra of the Wisdom Being (jñānasattva) who is well-characterized as both mind and non-mind— the commitment of body, speech, and mind—
while engaged in meditation and free from all conceptual constructions.
Through the recitation of the supreme commitment, there is the supreme recitation of the mantra:
OṂ VAJRAVAIROCANĪYE HŪṂ 2 PHAṬ SVĀHĀ | OṂ SARVABUDDHAḌĀKINĪYE HŪṂ 2 PHAṬ SVĀHĀ ||
One should employ the mantra of Pracaṇḍā and the others, joined with the *praṇava*, the name, and the syllables *hūṃ* and *phaṭ*, as the supreme recitation (*jāpa*).
When the recitation is completed, one should drink the supreme soma-juice as prescribed.
This is the supreme samaya of the equality that realizes all phenomena.
Subsequently, the thirty-seven supreme points of purification should be meditated upon.
One should enter the supreme mandala by means of the path of the selflessness of phenomena.
Having thus rested in the yoga of the perfection of wisdom, the yogin,
abiding in the state of non-appearance, relies upon the support of non-appearance.
In phenomena that are beyond conventional conduct, there is neither dharma nor the nature of dharma;
phenomena are dependently originated, devoid of intrinsic nature, and without characteristics.
Thus, abiding in the state of reality, one beholds with the eye of wisdom;
one should see the wheel of the seats (*pīṭhacakra*) with absolute certainty as being equal to atoms of dust.
Through the conceptualization of limbs within a hundred-thousandth part of the tip of a hair—
He beholds Heruka, together with the yoginīs, situated in the center of the bhaga.
By means of the procedure for a universal monarch (*cakravartin*), one should place Kākāsyā on the outside; she is presided over by Heruka and the others, and surrounded by the four ḍākinīs.
Having established mutual sovereignty, the practitioner of the yoga of Vajrasattva and the others attains the common siddhi of the yoginīs, the threefold yoga, the supreme commitment (samaya).
Having established threefold sovereignty, she shall wander the earth invisibly;
she is a wheel-turning queen of the great king of the triple world.
That great yogi attains accomplishment and gains sovereign power;
by means of this application of the method, he shall consume even forced death.
A wise person should slay those who commit the five acts of immediate retribution and those who are hostile;
otherwise, there will be a loss of accomplishment if one desires life as the fruit.
Through the yoga of animal sacrifice, the yoginī was entreated;
and the yogin should prepare the sacrificial pap (caru) together with his mother and sister.
Whether she be of the highest, middling, or even the lowest class, one should accomplish the supreme commitment together with a daughter by means of the application of the two organs.
Through the yoga of one's own tutelary deity, one enjoys the five objects of desire.
With the nature of Vārāhī, one should pierce the navel with the index finger.
Likewise, the goddesses of the wheel, such as Ḍākinī and the others, are of the form of emptiness.
Having caused her to enter through the nine gates, one should pierce the heart-lotus.
As soon as she is struck by the Yoginī, one should drink that excellent blood;
and having consumed what was struck, he shall indeed become a Buddha—there is no other way.
The ninth chapter, titled "The Instruction on the Signs and the Sequence of Attainment in the Yoginī-pīṭhas," from the Abhidhānottara.
